The Cape ground squirrel Geosciurus inauris exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect its adaptation to the semi-arid savannas of southern Africa. Gestation in this species lasts 45 days [tg = 45 days] under typical body temperatures of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], a duration that is relatively short for a rodent of its size and likely facilitates rapid replacement of offspring in a predator-rich environment. Pups emerge from the natal burrow after a suckling period that culminates in weaning at 50 days since birth [tx = 50 days since birth], a developmental milestone that marks the transition to independent foraging under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. The timing of these early life stages is closely tied to seasonal cycles of food abundance, ensuring that the energetic demands of late gestation and lactation coincide with peak resource availability.

Neonatal Cape ground squirrels are altricial at birth, weighing just 20 grams [Wwb = 20 grams], a modest initial mass that underscores the considerable energetic investment required during the ensuing lactation period. This low birth weight is typical of small-bodied sciurids that produce multiple offspring per litter. Over the course of the suckling interval, the mother's milk supports rapid somatic growth, and by the time of nutritional independence, the weanlings have reached a wet weight of 72.8 grams [Wwx = 72.8 grams]. This roughly three-and-a-half-fold increase in body mass over a relatively brief developmental window highlights the efficiency of maternal resource transfer and the importance of high-quality foraging habitats for the lactating female.

The species attains sexual maturity at a relatively advanced age for a rodent of its size. Puberty is reached at 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth], measured at a body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], a delay that allows for the completion of skeletal growth and the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves to support the high costs of reproduction. This pattern is consistent with a moderately slow life-history pace compared to many murine rodents of comparable adult mass. The prolonged juvenile period may also serve a social function, providing young individuals with an extended window for learning critical foraging and predator-avoidance behaviors within the complex matriarchal group structure that characterizes this species.

The maximum reproductive output of the Cape ground squirrel is modest when expressed on an annual basis. Females typically produce litters containing 2.2 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2.2 pups per litter], a value that, when combined with the average interbirth interval, translates into a relatively low annual fecundity relative to other ground-dwelling sciurids. This modest litter size is counterbalanced by the species' capacity to produce several litters within a single favorable breeding season. Adult female body mass, which ultimately stabilizes at 588 grams [Wwi = 588 grams], is likely a key determinant of reproductive output, as heavier individuals can allocate more resources to gestation and lactation. This asymptotic mass, known from extensive trapping studies, places Geosciurus inauris among the larger members of its genus.
